entities.name: Pascual de Andagoya
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Pascual de Andagoya (1495–1548), a Spanish Basque conquistador, served as a pivotal, albeit often overshadowed, figure in the early European exploration and colonization of South America. Born in Andagoya, Álava, he arrived in the Americas in 1514 as part of Pedrarias Dávila's large expedition to Castilla del Oro (modern-day Panama and Colombia). His explorations along the Pacific coast from Panama in 1522 were instrumental, leading him to the San Juan River in present-day Colombia and gathering the first concrete intelligence about a wealthy indigenous empire, 'Birú,' to the south—a name that would eventually evolve into 'Peru.' Andagoya's detailed reports and geographical findings directly preceded and informed Francisco Pizarro's more famous expeditions, laying the critical groundwork for the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire.

Andagoya's career began with participation in the founding of Panama City in 1519 and serving in various administrative and judicial roles within the nascent colony. His most significant undertaking commenced in 1522, when he led an expedition tasked with exploring the southern reaches of the newly discovered Pacific Ocean. Traveling by ship and canoe, he navigated the treacherous coastlines of modern-day Colombia, engaging with local indigenous groups and compiling extensive notes on their cultures, resources, and, crucially, their knowledge of a powerful state further south. Though a severe injury forced his premature return to Panama, his intelligence—detailing a land rich in gold and silver—ignited the ambitions of Pizarro, Diego de Almagro, and Hernando de Luque, who subsequently formed the 'Company of Levant' to pursue this promising new frontier.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Pascual de Andagoya's early explorations provided the crucial intelligence and geographical understanding that directly enabled Francisco Pizarro's conquest of the Inca Empire, fundamentally reshaping the course of South American history. His written 'Relación' also serves as an indispensable primary source for understanding the initial phase of Spanish colonization.
